issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not overturn concurrent factual findings by reweighing evidence when some evidence supports those findings and no substantial question of law permits interference.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the son had not consented to the gift, relying on evidence that his signature had been obtained deceitfully.
The High Court reassessed the evidence and reached a different conclusion about consent in a second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to reassess the evidence and reverse the concurrent finding on consent.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended, a second appeal is limited to cases involving a substantial question of law. Ladli Parshad Jaiswal v. The Karnal Distillery Co., Ltd. recognizes that a finding based on no evidence, a wrongful placement of the burden of proof, or a substantial procedural error may be disturbed, but an erroneous appreciation of evidence where some evidence exists does not permit a second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fi: The proceeding is a second appeal in which the lower courts made the same factual finding.
predicates.some_evidence_supports_lower_court_findi: The lower courts relied on some evidence in reaching their factual finding.
predicates.high_court_reweighed_evidence: The High Court reassessed the evidence to reach a different factual conclusion.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges a factual finding shared by the lower courts, and that finding has some evidentiary support, reweighing the evidence does not permit the finding to be disturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A gift of coparcenary immovable property that exceeds reasonable limits and is not for a recognized pious purpose cannot be sustained merely on the consent of one coparcener when other persons with an interest in the property have not consented.
material_facts: The disputed properties were found by the lower courts to be coparcenary property rather than the deceased coparcener’s self-acquired property.
The gift transferred a considerable portion of the coparcenary property and was not found to be for a recognized pious purpose.
The gift was made during the coparcener’s lifetime, after succession law provided for the deceased’s interest to devolve on specified female heirs if he died leaving them.
Even assuming the son consented, the other children did not consent to the gift.
issues.conclusion: The gift was invalid, and the gifted properties remained available for partition.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu father or managing member may gift immovable ancestral property only within reasonable limits for a recognized pious purpose. Ammathayee alias Perumalakkal v. Kumaresan states this limitation and recognizes a limited extension for a gift to a daughter fulfilling an antenuptial promise made when settling the terms of her marriage. Guramma v. Mallappa recognizes alienation with the consent of all coparceners in specified circumstances. Under the proviso to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, where the deceased leaves a female Class I heir, his interest devolves by succession rather than survivorship; consent from only the surviving coparcener therefore does not suffice to validate depletion of interests claimed by other heirs.

rule.if: coparcenary_immovable_property_gift and gift_exceeds_reasonable_limits and not gift_for_recognized_pious_purpose and deceased_left_class_i_female_heirs and not all_interested_heirs_consented

predicates.coparcenary_immovable_property_gift: A managing member gave away immovable property that belonged to the coparcenary.
predicates.gift_exceeds_reasonable_limits: The gift transferred a portion of the coparcenary property that was not within reasonable limits.
predicates.gift_for_recognized_pious_purpose: The gift was made for a recognized pious purpose.
predicates.deceased_left_class_i_female_heirs: The coparcener died leaving female heirs who were entitled to succeed to his interest.
predicates.all_interested_heirs_consented: Every person with an interest in the property consented to the gift.

issues.definition: If a managing member gives away an excessive portion of coparcenary immovable property for no recognized pious purpose, and interested female heirs survive without all interested persons consenting, the gift is invalid and the property remains available for partition.

issues.legal_issue: When a coparcener dies leaving female Class I heirs, the deceased’s interest devolves by succession rather than survivorship, and the applicable shares are determined by a notional partition followed by succession to that interest.
material_facts: The deceased coparcener died leaving a widow, daughters, and other Class I heirs, including an unmarried daughter and a surviving son who was the other coparcener.
The deceased’s mother and any predeceased son or brother were not surviving.
The High Court calculated the unmarried daughter’s share at the notional partition and each heir’s share in the deceased’s interest as an intestate heir.
The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court’s calculation of the parties’ shares.
issues.conclusion: The female-share provision applicable when joint family property passes to a single coparcener by survivorship did not apply to the deceased’s interest because that interest devolved by succession. The unmarried daughter received a share at the notional partition as well as a share as an heir, and the parties’ calculated shares were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives that Act overriding effect over inconsistent Hindu law. The proviso to Section 6 provides for succession rather than survivorship when a coparcener leaves a female Class I heir, while Explanation 1 to Section 6 requires a notional partition immediately before death. Section 8 of the Mysore Hindu Law Women’s Rights Act, 1933 provides the relevant female shares at partition; Section 8(1)(d) is superseded to the extent that the deceased’s interest does not pass by survivorship. Under Sections 8(1)(a) and 8(2)(c) of the Mysore Act, the unmarried daughter’s partition share is calculated by reference to her brother’s share. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum establishes that a female’s share at the notional partition is additional to her share as an heir; State of Maharashtra v. Narayan Rao is also cited on the effect of the notional partition.

predicates.coparcener_dies_with_class_i_female_heir: A coparcener dies leaving female heirs entitled to succeed to his interest.
predicates.deceased_interest_would_otherwise_pass_b: Absent the surviving female heirs, the deceased’s interest would pass to surviving coparceners by survivorship.
predicates.unmarried_daughter_qualifies_for_partiti: The deceased leaves an unmarried daughter who qualifies for a share when the family property is notionally partitioned.
predicates.heirs_succeed_to_deceased_interest: The deceased’s interest passes to his heirs by intestate succession.

issues.definition: When a coparcener dies leaving female heirs, any otherwise applicable survivorship-based share is unavailable, and shares are determined through a notional partition and succession to the deceased’s interest.
